title: 02 · Move a player: one file to reusable helpers
language: English / Thai guidance · English Python identifiers
assumptions: Proposed 90-minute lesson for C2–C3 readiness, assumed ages 10–15. Basic variables and if are checked; import/def and OOP are explicitly introduced.
Setup, event polling, asset loading and constructor/draw scaffolds are supplied and visible. Learners are assessed on movement, state ownership and guided extraction, not typing an engine.
Module extraction is guided first exposure. If the readiness gate fails, continue in one file and revisit extraction later; do not claim independent module fluency.

Schedule: original movement lesson 90 minutes, then a separate 45-minute sprite bridge BEFORE lesson 03. Do not squeeze both into one 90-minute class. Sprite readiness: explain Player.move and an instance attribute.

objectives.statement: Predict and implement held-key movement and draw a layered scene.
objectives.evidence: In your Player version, change self.speed from 180 to 240. Predict 12 pixels per dt=0.05. Test the same route to the landing pad and explain the precision trade-off.

objectives.statement: Explain a Player instance, its attributes, methods and self with independent positions.
objectives.evidence: Move a; explain why b stays still on an unseen trace.

objectives.statement: With guidance, extract scene helpers and distinguish import from calling them.
objectives.evidence: Point to definition, import and call; compare the same scene before/after.

objectives.statement: Select a top-down directional sprite using instance state, preserving facing at rest.
objectives.evidence: Explain an unseen two-player trace and implement the facing/image TODOs.

prerequisites: Assume only basic variables, if, and a little exposure to import/def. Show import pygame versus calling a function; trace x=160 then x+=18. Do not assume recall of classes from lesson 00.
entry_check: Assume only basic variables, if, and a little exposure to import/def. Show import pygame versus calling a function; trace x=160 then x+=18. Do not assume recall of classes from lesson 00.
materials: Tested desktop Python 3.12 + pygame-ce 2.5.8; keyboard; offline extracted student ZIP.
Projector, paper coordinate frame / trace sheet, and the supplied PNG assets.
prep: Install requirements before class. Run teacher 01_loop.py, 02_functions.py, main.py and modular/main.py. Confirm the same route, assets and 180 speed.
Distribute only student-project.zip. main.py must open a static scene. Modular stubs intentionally need learners to move their helpers before running.
Print worksheet and checkpoint map. Keep complete references and teacher answers hidden during prediction. Use the actual Python window for Run.
Prepare x/y cards for two players; rotate driver/navigator; save each working checkpoint before refactoring.

Before the bridge run teacher 04_sprites.py. Supply student 04_sprites.py, which already moves but has two sprite TODOs. View images/robot-directions.png as an atlas; code loads the four individual PNGs.

stages.name: Play · open one file
stages.teacher: Assume only basic variables, if, and a little exposure to import/def. Show import pygame versus calling a function; trace x=160 then x+=18. Do not assume recall of classes from lesson 00.
stages.prompt: Which line gets pygame ready to use? Does writing def call a function?
stages.learner: Open student main.py, identify import and the loop, run the static scene. Point to x/y and the landing pad.
stages.evidence: Each learner distinguishes import, definition and call with pointing or Thai speech.
stages.answer: import makes a module available. def stores a function definition; main() calls it. The launch guard is supplied setup, not an assessment target.
stages.misconception: Every line under def runs immediately.
stages.response: Compare a recipe with making it. Locate the final main() call before discussing any class.

stages.name: Predict · two tiny moves
stages.teacher: Display only the movement excerpt from teacher 01_loop.py, not its running result. Use dt=0.05 cards. Ask both partners before revealing.
stages.prompt: In 01_loop.py, x=160, speed=180 and Right is held. With dt=0.05, what is x after one update and two? What happens when the key is released?
stages.learner: Write or point to x after each of two updates; cite the += line.
stages.evidence: Predicts 169,178 and explains why release gives dx=0.
stages.answer: 169 then 178. dx=1, so each update adds 9. When released dx=0, so x stays put. tick returns milliseconds; dividing by 1000 gives seconds. The 0.05 cap avoids a huge jump after a pause.
stages.response: Multiply one dt card by speed, then add to the position.

stages.name: Run · watch the loop
stages.teacher: Run the unchanged teacher 01_loop.py. Hold/release arrows; close and restart. Compare direction and stop behaviour with the exact paper trace; live elapsed time will vary.
stages.prompt: What keeps drawing when you release the key?
stages.learner: Observe the same reference and explain input -> update -> background -> player -> flip.
stages.evidence: Separates a stopped player from a stopped game loop.
stages.answer: The loop continues. dx/dy become zero; the position stays fixed while frames redraw.
stages.misconception: Use input() or sleep() to wait for a key.
stages.response: Act out the cycle; blocking prevents the scene and window events from updating.

stages.name: Investigate · name the drawing jobs
stages.teacher: Learners fill two movement TODO lines in main.py; begin horizontally. Save my_loop.py. Compare 02_functions.py: move background lines into draw_scene and repeated image loading into load_sprite. Explain parameters and return with one image path. Do not introduce Player yet.
stages.prompt: Which helper runs once, and which runs every frame? Why clear the screen first?
stages.learner: Carry their own movement and background into the function checkpoint; call helpers and test unchanged behaviour.
stages.evidence: Identifies load_sprite before the loop and draw_scene inside it; a complete scene still renders.
stages.answer: Load each asset once after set_mode; draw_scene clears and draws every frame. return gives the resized image to the caller. Draw the player afterwards so it is not erased.
stages.misconception: Moving code into def means it still executes without a call.
stages.response: Point from the call and arguments to the matching parameters; temporarily omit the call and predict the missing scene.

stages.name: Investigate · give the player its own state
stages.teacher: Save my_functions.py. Reveal one part of 03_player.py at a time: class as description, Player(...) as construction, __init__ stores state, self names the receiving object, move/draw are methods. Supply constructor/draw; students adapt their movement using self. Swap pair roles after 9 minutes. Demonstrate object_probe.py only after predictions.
stages.prompt: nova.move(1,0,0.05) changes whose x? If pip starts at 500, what happens to pip?
stages.learner: Make Player.move work in one main.py. Trace two separate objects on paper; explain image versus position.
stages.evidence: Movement works and each learner explains self and unchanged pip.x.
stages.answer: nova.x becomes 169; pip.x stays 500. Both share the class definition, but each owns x/y/speed. A method is a function belonging to an object.
stages.misconception: A class is a picture; self moves every player; importing scene draws the scene automatically.
stages.response: Point to the data and method separately. Trace a.move with cards labelled a and b. Import scene without calling anything; then call draw_scene once. The picture is only one attribute.

stages.name: Modify · tune the movement
stages.teacher: Use the completed one-file Player version. Keep the target and start fixed while testing speed. Show teacher_example.py only after the learner attempts a change.
stages.prompt: In your Player version, change self.speed from 180 to 240. Predict 12 pixels per dt=0.05. Test the same route to the landing pad and explain the precision trade-off.
stages.learner: Predict 9 versus 12 pixels per 0.05s; test and record one control difference.
stages.evidence: Explains a precision/speed trade-off using a test, not just colour changes.
stages.answer: 240*0.05=12. Faster travel may make stopping accurately harder; accept different preferences supported by observation.
stages.misconception: Changing a separate speed variable changes self.speed automatically.
stages.response: Locate the exact attribute read by move. Change that value and retest.

stages.name: Investigate · reuse your helper with import
stages.teacher: Guided refactor: save my_player.py, transfer completed code into modular/main.py, MOVE load_sprite/draw_scene into modular/scene.py (with import pygame). Remove the local definitions and use from scene import load_sprite, draw_scene. Keep window creation and loop in main.py. The asset path goes up one folder because this checkpoint is in modular/. Test the same start/speed/target.
stages.prompt: Does importing draw_scene draw anything? Which call still needs to stay in the loop?
stages.learner: Replace the intentional stubs with their own helpers; run python modular/main.py and compare behaviour.
stages.evidence: Can identify the definition file, import line and call; extraction leaves movement unchanged.
stages.answer: Import makes definitions available; draw_scene(screen,pad,pad_position) still runs in the loop. scene.py defines helpers without opening a window. No circular import is needed.
stages.misconception: Copy the entire game loop into scene.py or leave two competing helper definitions.
stages.response: Move only the two def blocks. Compare before/after and restart; if time is short, retain the working one-file version and schedule extraction practice.

stages.name: Make · design a docking scene
stages.teacher: Allow either working one-file or modular version. Plan 3 minutes, build 6, swap/playtest 3, save 1. Require one movement decision and one background route cue; visual decoration alone is not the goal.
stages.prompt: Choose a starting position, landing-pad position and speed to design a precision docking challenge. Draw a background route using your scene helper. Ask a partner to stop on the pad; use their observation to revise one movement choice. No collision or win detection is supplied.
stages.learner: Design and test; report one observed problem and a revision.
stages.evidence: A partner can try the route and the author explains a behaviour change.
stages.answer: Valid outcomes vary. Use visual docking by stopping on the pad. Do not claim automatic scoring or collision.
stages.misconception: A new background colour proves movement understanding.
stages.response: Ask for a new start/speed prediction and a repeatable route test.

stages.name: Grow · explain independently
stages.teacher: Use 4 minutes for individual checks, 2 to save the whole folder and 1 for a next step. Check each partner. Mark prompted versus independent; do not infer mastery from a runnable file.
stages.prompt: New case: a.x=200, a.speed=120; a.move(-1,0,0.5). What is a.x? If b.x=500, does it change? Name the two lines needed to use draw_scene from scene.py.
stages.learner: Trace one unseen movement, explain self and identify import versus call. Save the whole project.
stages.evidence: Three separately recorded checks: movement, object ownership, helper reuse.
stages.answer: a.x=140; b.x stays 500 because self is a for this call. Use from scene import draw_scene and then draw_scene(screen,pad,pad_position) inside the loop. Import makes the helper available; the call draws this frame. The direct method trace uses dt=0.5; the running loop caps dt at 0.05.
stages.misconception: The unchanged second object also moves because it is a Player.
stages.response: Return to two labelled position cards; then give a different direction/value.

stages.name: Bridge · what is a sprite?
stages.teacher: Start a separate 45-minute session after the movement exit check. Keep the saved Player project. Show four directional PNGs and the teacher 04_sprites.py excerpt without running. A sprite is an image representing a game object; our Player owns position and chooses its image. These are direction frames, not a walking animation.
stages.prompt: Start facing down. Predict the picture after Right, release, Up. Does choosing a picture move x or y?
stages.learner: Point to a direction card for each input and explain the camera looking down at the floor.
stages.evidence: Separates position, direction and picture before seeing the game.
stages.answer: right, right, up. Selecting an image does not move position; move changes x/y separately.
stages.misconception: A sprite is a class, or changing the picture moves the character.
stages.response: Hold one paper robot at the same coordinate and swap the picture. Then move the paper without swapping it.

stages.name: Run · look from above
stages.teacher: Run the complete teacher 04_sprites.py unchanged. Compare the prediction. Show up/down/left/right, release and Up+Right. Explain that student 04_sprites.py moves but deliberately keeps the down picture until its TODOs are completed.
stages.prompt: Which part of the robot do you see when it travels up? What happens after release?
stages.learner: Test the exact sequence; rotate driver/navigator.
stages.evidence: Recognises the back view and persistent facing at rest.
stages.answer: Up shows the back/top of the robot. Release stops movement but preserves the last facing. Up+Right moves diagonally and shows up.
stages.misconception: Up should show the same front-facing portrait rotated sideways.
stages.response: Use the sheet as a camera model: the camera stays above; the character changes its world direction.

stages.name: Investigate · a picture wardrobe
stages.teacher: Introduce one dictionary lookup: sprites["up"] selects the image stored under the key up. Read the four explicit entries before introducing self.sprites[self.facing]. Trace __init__, the if/elif chain in move, then draw. Load images once outside the loop. All frames share a 64px canvas and centre; draw chooses the image every frame. Do not introduce inheritance or pygame.sprite.Sprite.
stages.prompt: Which attribute remembers direction? Why is there no final else setting down?
stages.learner: Annotate key, image value, facing attribute and selected image. Complete the two student TODO areas using the trace.
stages.evidence: Explains that self.facing belongs to this Player and remains unchanged without direction input.
stages.answer: self.facing stores a string such as "up". self.sprites maps that key to an image. No matching branch leaves the previous value; a final else would reset it on release.
stages.misconception: The direction string itself is an image, or all Player objects share facing.
stages.response: Use four labelled pockets and picture cards. Give two players separate facing cards while sharing the same picture library.

stages.name: Modify · who wins on a diagonal?
stages.teacher: After the core TODOs work, ask pairs to change branch order so horizontal direction wins diagonals. Predict first, then test Up+Right. Keep x/y movement unchanged. Swap roles halfway.
stages.prompt: What should change, and what should stay the same?
stages.learner: Move dx branches before dy branches, then compare position and facing.
stages.evidence: Same diagonal travel; right picture instead of up.
stages.answer: if/elif takes the first matching branch. Horizontal-first shows right for dx=1,dy=-1. Movement still updates both axes.
stages.misconception: Choosing one facing direction prevents diagonal movement.
stages.response: Trace the facing chain and the two position assignments as separate jobs.

stages.name: Make · face the docking station
stages.teacher: Learners choose two stop locations and a required facing at each. Plan 2 minutes, code/test 5, partner feedback 2, save 1. Use visual checking only; collision and scoring come later.
stages.prompt: Design a route where stopping in the right place is not enough: the robot must face the station too.
stages.learner: Draw two target cues, choose a facing policy, and ask a partner to test stop-and-face behaviour.
stages.evidence: A route with two deliberate facing choices and one revision after feedback.
stages.answer: Accept different routes. Require correct image selection, no snap to down on release, and an explanation of the chosen diagonal rule.
stages.misconception: A coloured background alone demonstrates sprite state.
stages.response: Ask the learner to demonstrate a direction change followed by release and explain the saved attribute.

stages.name: Grow · whose direction changed?
stages.teacher: Assess each learner independently, then save the whole folder. Use the original vertical-first reference for this exit. Gate lesson 03 on movement and facing explanations; provide another trace if prompted.
stages.prompt: a and b start facing down. Only a.move(-1,0,0.05), then a.move(0,0,0.05). Which image does each draw? If a next moves Up+Left, which image wins?
stages.learner: Answer with direction cards and point to the attribute and lookup in code.
stages.evidence: a left, b down; then a up. Explains instance ownership and idle memory.
stages.answer: a shows left at rest; b still down. Up+Left shows up in the original vertical-first chain. Shared images do not share self.facing.
stages.misconception: Stopping resets both players or the second object turns too.
stages.response: Return to two separate facing cards; trace only the object named before .move.

differentiation.support: Complete horizontal movement in the visible single-file loop first. Provide dt=0.05 counters. Use the supplied constructor and draw method; learners implement move. If not ready, keep helpers local and revisit extraction next session. Sprite bridge: use labelled direction cards and first implement left/right only; supply the dictionary and introduce one lookup at a time.
differentiation.core: In your Player version, change self.speed from 180 to 240. Predict 12 pixels per dt=0.05. Test the same route to the landing pad and explain the precision trade-off.
differentiation.stretch: Create a second Player with a different start/speed. Move only one and explain independent state. Then discuss faster diagonal movement; normalization is optional, not a prerequisite. Sprite stretch: draw a second Player with the same image dictionary but independent facing; rotate only one.
differentiation.access: Accept Thai oral explanations or a paper trace. Enlarge code and reduce typing with the starter. Use untimed practice and a no-flash option. Distinguish keyboard difficulty from understanding.
differentiation.late_arrival: Open student 03_player.py with the teacher and trace the supplied constructor. Complete one movement direction; compare one helper call. Assess only demonstrated work.
differentiation.short_route: 60 minutes: entry 5, Predict/Run 8, helpers 10, Player 15, Modify/Make 15, exit/save 7. Defer hands-on extraction; teacher previews import and schedules practice. O3 is not yet independently demonstrated. Sprite bridge short route: 25 minutes = Predict/Run 5, Investigate 10, Modify 5, exit/save 5. Defer the docking Make to the next session before collection.
differentiation.fallback: Use two labelled Player cards and the exact movement code. Move a paper robot over a coordinate background; place helper-definition/import/call cards in order. Graphics and imports remain unverified without Python. For sprites, swap printed atlas frames on a coordinate board; keep separate facing cards for two players.

assessment.task: x=200, speed=120, dx=-1, dt=0.5 in a direct move call. Predict x. Explain why scene clear must precede the player draw.
assessment.expected: 140. Clear after the player would erase it; dt here is a direct trace value, not the loop-capped dt.
assessment.next_step: Complete horizontal movement in the visible single-file loop first. Provide dt=0.05 counters. Use the supplied constructor and draw method; learners implement move. If not ready, keep helpers local and revisit extraction next session.

assessment.task: a starts at 200 and b at 500. Only a.move(-1,0,0.5) is called at speed 120. Explain both positions and self.
assessment.expected: a=140, b=500; self is a in this call. The class describes both but does not share their x.
assessment.next_step: Point to the data and method separately. Trace a.move with cards labelled a and b. Import scene without calling anything; then call draw_scene once. The picture is only one attribute.

assessment.task: Identify where draw_scene is defined, imported and called. Predict what happens if its call is removed.
assessment.expected: Definition in scene.py; from scene import draw_scene in main.py; call inside the loop. Import alone does not draw. Without the call the scene is not cleared/redrawn.
assessment.next_step: If prompted, repeat moving one helper next session before adding modules.

assessment.task: a and b start facing down. Only a.move(-1,0,0.05), then a.move(0,0,0.05). Which image does each draw? If a next moves Up+Left, which image wins?
assessment.expected: a shows left at rest; b still down. Up+Left shows up in the original vertical-first chain. Shared images do not share self.facing.
assessment.next_step: Return to two separate facing cards; trace only the object named before .move.

reflection: I expected… The test showed… I changed… Next I will…
parent_prompt: Today: [mechanic]. Evidence: [actual independent action/explanation and support used]. Next: [one step from that evidence]. Do not infer achievement from the planned lesson.
next_lesson: Complete the 45-minute sprite bridge (04_sprites.py) before Collect once. Retrieve: position, facing and selected image are different state/jobs. Lesson 03 currently uses studio.py: map its update(dt)/draw() to our move/draw methods explicitly. Keep this saved class-based checkpoint; do not paste the entire file into the older scaffold.

motto.play: Guide a robot towards a landing pad.
motto.think: In 01_loop.py, x=160, speed=180 and Right is held. With dt=0.05, what is x after one update and two? What happens when the key is released?
motto.code: Start with the visible loop in one main.py. Name load_sprite and draw_scene, call each at the right time, then group x/y/speed/image and move/draw inside Player. self means the receiving player. Only then move scene helpers to scene.py and import them.
motto.create: Choose a starting position, landing-pad position and speed to design a precision docking challenge. Draw a background route using your scene helper. Ask a partner to stop on the pad; use their observation to revise one movement choice. No collision or win detection is supplied.
motto.grow: New case: a.x=200, a.speed=120; a.move(-1,0,0.5). What is a.x? If b.x=500, does it change? Name the two lines needed to use draw_scene from scene.py.

resources.title: Setup and checkpoint run commands
resources.use: Install before class; distinguish teacher and student routes.
resources.content:
LESSON 02 — no studio.py
Extract the whole kit. Keep images/ beside main.py; modular/ remains inside this folder.
Install once in your Python environment: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
Use the same python command/environment to run the files. Tested dependency: pygame-ce 2.5.8.
Do not name any file pygame.py. Run from a terminal, not a browser.

STUDENT ROUTE (main.py begins as a working static scene):
1. python main.py — add movement and a background route at the TODOs.
2. Save your work as my_loop.py. Read 02_functions.py, then copy your own code into the helpers. Save as main.py when ready.
3. Save my_functions.py. Use 03_player.py as the next main.py; adapt YOUR movement into Player.move. The supplied constructor and draw method are scaffolds.
4. Save my_player.py. Copy your completed methods into modular/main.py. Move your two scene helper definitions into modular/scene.py, replacing the TODO stubs. Run python modular/main.py. This stage intentionally raises NotImplementedError until you move the helpers.

TEACHER ROUTE:
python 01_loop.py -> python 02_functions.py -> python main.py -> python modular/main.py
Each checkpoint is complete and separately runnable. main.py is the one-file Player reference. reference.py and starter.py are launch aliases. teacher_example.py changes speed to 240.
python object_probe.py prints independent object positions without opening a game window.

Arrows move; Escape or close quits. Close/re-run to restart. No H or R shortcuts in this lesson. The landing pad is a visual target, not a collision detector.
Position is the 64px sprite centre in an 800x600 window; clamp x to 32..768, y to 32..568. speed is pixels/second, dt is seconds capped at 0.05 in the loop. Opposite keys: Right/Down win in this simple example; diagonals are faster.
load_sprite runs once after the window is created. draw_scene runs each frame, clearing first, then ground/route/pad. Player.draw runs last.
No inheritance, pygame.sprite.Sprite, Vector2 or separate engine is required.

5. SPRITE BRIDGE (separate 45-minute session before lesson 03): python 04_sprites.py. Student: movement/setup are supplied prior learning; complete facing if/elif and dictionary lookup TODOs. Teacher: complete reference. Start facing down; arrows move/turn; release remembers direction. Vertical wins diagonals; right/down win opposite keys. At a wall, facing follows input even if position is clamped. Escape/close quits; re-run resets. All four images load once and draw centred at 64px. Dictionary: direction key -> image value. No inheritance or walk-cycle animation yet.

resources.title: One file to modules: checkpoint map
resources.use: Keep beside the editor while changing structure.
resources.content:
CHECKPOINT MAP
1. main.py: student static scene -> write movement and a background route. Teacher reference: 01_loop.py.
2. 02_functions.py: named jobs in the SAME file. Move your own code; save my_loop.py first.
3. 03_player.py: Player owns x/y/speed/image. Adapt move; save my_functions.py first. Teacher reference: main.py.
4. modular/main.py + scene.py: import only your two scene helpers. Keep class and loop in main. Save my_player.py first.
Compare behaviour after each refactor. Do not overwrite your only working copy.
5. SPRITE BRIDGE (separate 45-minute session before lesson 03): python 04_sprites.py. Student: movement/setup are supplied prior learning; complete facing if/elif and dictionary lookup TODOs. Teacher: complete reference. Start facing down; arrows move/turn; release remembers direction. Vertical wins diagonals; right/down win opposite keys. At a wall, facing follows input even if position is clamped. Escape/close quits; re-run resets. All four images load once and draw centred at 64px. Dictionary: direction key -> image value. No inheritance or walk-cycle animation yet.
